newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian apple sales plummet after blight alarm.
newsitem.headline: Australian apple sales plummet after blight alarm.

text.p: Sales of Australian apples and pears have dropped dramatically since a New Zealand scientist reported that two apple trees in a Melbourne park were infected by fire blight disease, farmers said on Wednesday.
Jon Durham, chief executive of the Australian Apple and Pear Growers' Association, told Reuters domestic apple and pear orders had plummeted by 40 percent over the past 24 hours.

This accelerated the sales decline, which initially emerged at 10 percent after the fire blight scare emerged two weeks ago when a visiting New Zealander said he had found fire blight in Melbourne's Botanic Gardens.
"That (sales drop is) of enormous concern," Durham said.

The scientist's claim has led to a war of words between Australia and New Zealand, with Australian farmers crying foul. Fire blight is a bacterial disease which can devastate orchards, although the fruit is not affected.

Conciliatory statements on Tuesday by Australia's Primary Industries Minister John Anderson did little to erase Australian concern that fire blight sufferer New Zealand could be trying to rock its Australian competition.
"If it's not a New Zealand plot to damage Australia, they've been inordinately successful doing so without trying," Durham said.
The Australian apple and pear industry is worth around A$360 million a year.

"I can understand how upset Australian growers are about this. But...it means Australia will be looking at stopping the spread of the disease earlier than might otherwise have been the case," Lockwood Smith, New Zealand's minister of international trade, said in a statement from Wellington.
While only 15-20 percent of Australia's annual apple crop is exported as fresh fruit, mostly to Asia, the fire blight scare has arisen at a critical time for exporters.
After 20 years of trying to gain access to a very cautious Japanese market, Australian producers met Japanese authorities on May 2 to discuss the export of Fuji apples to Japan.
"There were some questions raised but subsequent to those being addressed satisfactorily it was likely that access to (Japan) would have been approved in coming months," Durham said.

Virtually fire blight-free Japan was potentially a "very lucrative market", with a big population willing to pay an enormous price for apples. The scare certainly would delay the process of getting Australian apples into Japan, he said.

While fire blight sufferers New Zealand and the United States both had access to Japan's apple market, protocols on their exports were "horrendously difficult to comply with and render the business virtually uneconomic", Durham said.

Victorian apples and pears are still blocked from all other Australian states while an intensive testing program continues, but the other Australian states have promised to progressively lift bans on an area-by-area basis as clearances arise.

Mike Kinsella, a Victorian state official in charge of the tests, told Reuters three teams were testing full-time in the north and south of Victoria. Tests were also being conducted in parks and private gardens around Melbourne.
He said no evidence of fire blight had yet been found, although it would take some time for tests to be concluded.
Kinsella said the procedure used in the Melbourne Botanic Gardens case was an "in-house New Zealand method which has some cloud over it".
Apart from its fresh fruit exports, Australia is also the world's largest exporter of canned pears, supplying about 39 percent of the international market.
